notes.meaning: Manasseh was only twelve years old when he became king of Judah, and he ended up ruling longer than any other king in Jerusalem. For the first several years, he served as co-ruler alongside his godly father, Hezekiah. Even though a long reign was often viewed as a sign of God's blessing, Manasseh spent most of those decades promoting wicked practices.

Instead of copying his father's faith, Manasseh plunged Judah into the evil customs of the pagan nations God had long ago driven out of Canaan. A parent's strong faith cannot be passed down automatically, and Manasseh made a deliberate choice to rebel. He embraced the very sins that had brought God's judgment on the land centuries before.

Manasseh tore down his father's good work by rebuilding the local hilltop shrines and making altars for the false god Baal and wooden poles for the goddess Asherah. He also began worshipping the sun, moon, and stars, adopting pagan astrology from Babylon and Assyria. He pushed Judah into foreign superstitions that went far beyond what earlier kings had practiced.

Manasseh boldly brought his idolatry inside the temple of the Lord. God had set this house apart in Jerusalem as the place where His name would be honored forever. Setting up pagan altars in that sacred building was an open display of contempt for the true God.

Manasseh set up altars to the stars and planets across both courtyards of the temple. These public spaces were meant for God's people to gather for prayer and pure worship. Instead, Manasseh replaced the worship of the Creator with the worship of the created skies right outside God's dwelling.

Manasseh sank into terrible darkness by burning his own children as human sacrifices in the valley outside Jerusalem. He pursued hidden knowledge through fortune-telling, spells, and consulting spirits of the dead. These dreadful practices directly broke God's law and provoked His righteous anger.

Manasseh placed a carved wooden image of the goddess Asherah directly inside the temple building itself. God had specifically chosen Jerusalem and this holy house out of all Israel's tribal territories to place His name. Putting a pagan idol inside the sanctuary was a direct insult to the Lord who dwelt there.

God reminded the people of His ancient promise that Israel would never be driven from the Promised Land if they obeyed His law. Their safety and peace depended on careful obedience to the commands given through Moses. By choosing willful rebellion instead, they put the entire nation at risk of exile.

Under Manasseh's leadership, the people of Judah did worse things than the pagan nations God had destroyed before them. Judah had God's word and temple, so their guilt was far greater than the ignorance of the heathen. A ruler's bad example can quickly drag an entire nation into spiritual ruin.

The Lord sent prophets to warn Manasseh and his subjects of the disaster that their sins would bring. God showed great patience by offering warnings instead of striking them with immediate judgment. Yet the king and the people hardened their hearts and refused to pay attention.

Because Manasseh would not listen, God brought the Assyrian army against him, likely under King Esarhaddon. The Assyrian commanders captured Manasseh, put a painful ring or hook through his nose, bound him in bronze chains, and took him away as a prisoner to Babylon. The proud king was stripped of his royal glory and completely humiliated.

Locked away in a foreign prison, Manasseh finally recognized the horror of his rebellion against God. Instead of growing bitter or stubborn under his suffering, he pleaded for mercy and deeply humbled himself before the God of his fathers. Pain and affliction can be a severe mercy when they break our pride and lead us back to God.

God heard Manasseh's desperate plea, accepted his repentance, and miraculously brought him back to Jerusalem as king. Through this wonderful deliverance, Manasseh learned by personal experience that the Lord alone is the true God. This shows that God's grace can forgive and restore even the worst sinner who truly turns to Him.

After his return, Manasseh took steps to fortify Jerusalem, building a strong outer wall that ran from the Gihon spring toward the Fish Gate. He raised the defensive wall around the hill of Ophel and stationed commanders in the fortified towns throughout Judah. His spiritual change bore practical fruit in caring for the protection of his people.

Manasseh proved his repentance was genuine by throwing out the foreign idols and the Asherah image from the temple. He also removed the pagan altars he had constructed across Jerusalem and dumped them outside the city walls. Real repentance always means getting rid of the things that led us into sin.

Manasseh rebuilt the Lord's broken altar and offered fellowship and thank offerings to express gratitude for God's forgiveness. Then he used his royal authority to command all the people of Judah to serve the Lord alone. Having once led the nation into sin, he now did everything he could to lead them back to God.

Even though the people abandoned idols, they still offered sacrifices at local hilltop altars rather than travelling to the temple. Manasseh could destroy the public idols, but he could not quickly wipe out decades of bad spiritual habits among the people. It is much easier to lead others into sin than to guide them back to full obedience.

The writer points to outside royal records for other details about Manasseh's life, including his humble prayer and the warnings given by God's prophets. Those ancient state records preserved the fuller story of how God dealt with this king. Although those original source books are lost today, Scripture preserves everything necessary to show God's saving mercy.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: The Orthodox Church includes an ancient writing called the Prayer of Manasseh in the Old Testament, using it in its Great Compline service.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Catholic Church places the ancient Prayer of Manasseh in an appendix to the Latin Vulgate, treating it as a pious ancient text rather than inspired Scripture.

notes.meaning: Another ancient book, the Records of the Seers, recorded Manasseh's prayer and how God graciously answered him. It also kept track of the king's unfaithfulness and the places where he had set up idols before his heart was changed. God made sure that the king's deep repentance was remembered alongside his worst sins as a testimony to divine grace.

Manasseh died and was buried privately in his palace garden rather than in the historic royal tombs of David's line. His passing ended a long fifty-five-year reign that turned from terrible idolatry to personal repentance. His son Amon then took the throne of Judah.

Amon was twenty-two years old when he became king of Judah, but his reign lasted only two short years. Unlike his father, who had many decades and eventually turned to God, Amon had very little time on the throne. His brief rule was marked entirely by wickedness.

Amon followed the evil pattern of his father's early years rather than the humility of his father's old age. He brought back the worship of the carved idols that Manasseh had cast away, offering sacrifices to them with full devotion. Having seen the painful consequences of his father's idolatry, Amon had no excuse for repeating those sins.

Amon copied his father's sinful deeds, but he refused to copy his father's repentance. Instead of humbling himself before God, he piled sin upon sin and made his guilt even heavier. It is not sin alone that destroys a person, but the stubborn refusal to repent and ask for God's mercy.

After only two years of rule, Amon was assassinated in his own palace by his royal servants. His wicked life came to a sudden end, leaving him no opportunity for a late repentance. Presuming that one can safely delay turning to God until old age is a dangerous mistake.

The people of Judah rose up, executed the assassins who had murdered King Amon, and made his eight-year-old son Josiah the new king. By stepping in, the people preserved the royal line of David according to God's ancient covenant. Out of Amon's tragic reign, God brought forth Josiah, who would become one of Judah's most godly rulers.
